On October 27, 2019 the Agricultural Advancement Act has implemented a sweeping change to China’s Agricultural Policy.

The Netherlands’ reviews of farming infrastructure have brought about some improvements, but these have only highlighted the poor efficiency of China’s agriculture, and the large amount of food that goes to waste is not only a tragedy, but it is stifling growth in Agriculture..

One major reason for this is because, unlike manufactured goods, Agriculture was never liberalized. The land is owned by the state, and improvements have been slow to say the least.

In an effort to bring vital change to China as it continues to develop, the Communist Party has put to law the Agricultural Advancement Act, which will do the following:

  1. Implement Land Lease Contracts. Land Lease Contracts will indicate that the holder has an ownership of the land for the purpose of agricultural production. Contracts can be traded, but in the end it is beholden to the Chinese state. Farmers who currently work land are to be given Land Lease Contracts for their lands, which they can either keep or sell. Farmers are being informed about the value of their land so that they can make wise decisions with their LLCs. LLCs will give farmers more control over their land and also help prevent officials from seizing farmers’ land without warrant. Farmers will also own the produce of their land and can choose to sell it where, how, and when they would like.
  2. Allow for a more open Food and Agricultural Sector. With this happening China is likely to start becoming a net food Importer rather than Exporter, at least until domestic production catches up sufficiently to abroad. Foreign companies are allowed to purchase Land Lease Contracts from farmers so long as at least half the food goes to the Chinese market rather than being taken back abroad.
  3. Increase budget for rural infrastructure. Although over the past several years rural infrastructure has been something Wu Qiang’s government has been paying attention to, it is now time to improve this so that the value of the land, and its potential productivity, can increase.

These reforms are relatively radical to many, but it was met with great praise from the hundreds of millions of farmers in China who now have more contractual control over their land. Many have cited hopes that they may be able to sell their property and move to better locations, while others are hoping to rent out their land and take in profits over time. Still, some wish to remain as they have, but hopefully under better conditions.

Economists around the world are scrambling for the opportunities. Most cite that China becoming a net importer will be a shock to the world market and indicate that prices of food will likely rise somewhat in the rest of the world as a result. However, agricultural giants from around the world as well as large Chinese corporations looking to diversify what they do are looking to get a hold of farmland so that they can take advantage of the newly opened market. Most say that things will be a little bit difficult for now, but in the future the efficiency of China’s agriculture will likely rise close to places such as South Korea over the next couple of decades.

Another reason for this is the increasing wealth of the urban natives of China contributing to a burgeoning middle class, one that demands things that China produces, allowing for manufacturers to begin to pay attention to domestic markets.

Proposed Roll on the effects of the legislation: 1d10

1: Chaos ensues as farmers make poor choices in their selling, leading to volatility in the agricultural sector and a decrease in confidence for the administration.

2: Farmers largely refuse to sell their land. Although the infrastructure improvements and property incentives are there, improvements in efficiency will be very slow. Questions are raised as to the Wu Qiang administration’s judgment.

3-5: The legislation goes bumpily. A flood of buyers occurs too soon, sending the agricultural sector spinning for a couple years before evening out to a burgeoning marketplace.

6-7: Large Chinese and International companies pay well for the land and the agricultural sector begins to expand with the liberalization.

8-9: Large and medium-sized Chinese and International companies, as well as startups, pay well for the land and begin to increase agricultural efficiency quickly. Some groups even help to improve the infrastructure to try to get started more quickly. The Wu Qiang administration is praised for its good judgment.

10: A beautiful marketplace of small, medium, and large businesses, old and new, Chinese and International, take up the land and begin to improve the efficiency of Chinese agriculture quickly. Some of the larger companies even help with infrastructure improvements to try to get things going as quickly as possible. Confidence in the Wu Qiang administration increases as China’s markets surge.
